Thank you for the info.=0AThe affordable laser range finders I found had a =
very limited range with max readings usually around 1km, which is insuffici=
ent in our case (most of our sightings are further away form the ship than =
1 km). =0A=0ARegarding the icebergs, in most cases it is not a big iceberg =
that blocks the view of the horizon but a field a small ice floes of differ=
ent sizes so the use of a radar is not often possible.=0A=0AAny other idea =

ey aren't very useful. A less expensive laser range finder will do better t=

the horizon distance with reticle binoculars.=0A>=0A>--jeff=0A>=0A>On 11/8/=
2011 5:57 AM, Magaly CHAMBELLANT wrote:=0A>> Good Day,=0A>> =0A>> I am part=
of a team doing ship-based line-transect whale surveys in Antarctica and w=
e have some trouble estimating the distances because the horizon is often b=
locked from view by icebergs. We were thinking of using laser range finders=
but considering the time the traget stays in view, the distance from the s=
hip and the sea state, we would need a military grade laser range finder an=
d our budget does not allow this kind of device. I was wondering if the use=
of=A0 a clinometer would work since it seems the horizon is not necessaril=
